title: Transition Strips From Vinyl Plank to Tile, Carpet and Hardwood
meta: Vinyl plank meets tile, carpet or hardwood? Use a T-molding, reducer or end cap, leave the gap, never pin the floating floor. Wills Flooring's Seattle guide.
keywords: vinyl plank transition to tile, vinyl plank to carpet transition strip, LVP to hardwood transition, T-molding vs reducer vinyl plank, vinyl plank installation Seattle

blocks.lead: Vinyl plank meets other floors with one of four strips: a T-molding when both sides are the same height, a reducer when the vinyl is higher, an end cap against carpet, and a flush or overlap threshold against hardwood or tall tile.
blocks.detail: The rule underneath all four is the same: a floating vinyl floor must be free to move, so the strip covers the expansion gap without pinning the planks. Wills Flooring installs vinyl plank at $2.50 per sq ft; transitions are quoted with the job.

blocks.html: Almost every vinyl plank job in Seattle runs into another floor somewhere. A Ballard bungalow keeps its original fir in the living room and gets vinyl in the kitchen. A Capitol Hill condo has tile at the entry and carpet in the bedrooms. A West Seattle basement meets a slab step at the garage door. The plank itself is easy; the doorways are where jobs go wrong, because a transition is both trim and a structural detail that lets a floating floor breathe.

blocks.text: Why transitions matter more on vinyl plank than on other floors

blocks.title: The floating floor rule:
blocks.text: Click-lock vinyl plank is not attached to the subfloor. It expands and contracts as one sheet with temperature and, on WPC cores, humidity. If a strip is screwed or glued through the planks, the floor cannot move, and it buckles at the doorway or gaps at the far wall. Every strip fastens to the subfloor or a track, never to the vinyl.
The four transition types and when each one belongs

items.title: T-molding
items.text: A T-shaped strip whose top bridges two floors of equal height, with the stem in the gap between them. Used vinyl-to-tile and vinyl-to-hardwood when both surfaces land within about 1/8 in. Snaps into a track fastened to the subfloor, so the planks stay free.

items.title: Reducer
items.text: A wedge that ramps down from the vinyl to a lower floor, such as sheet vinyl, thin tile or a bare slab in a Seattle basement. Most vinyl plank sits 5 to 8 mm high, so a reducer is common where it meets a thinner old floor.

items.title: End cap (square nose)
items.text: Finishes the vinyl edge where it meets carpet, a sliding door track, a hearth or an exterior threshold. The carpet is tucked and stapled up to the cap, not under it. This is the correct strip for vinyl-to-carpet, and the one most often replaced with a metal bar that looks like a rental.

items.title: Threshold, flush or overlap
items.text: A taller strip used against a floor higher than the vinyl, such as porcelain over a mud bed or old 3/4 in hardwood. It steps up rather than down. Where vinyl meets original wood, a hardwood threshold milled and stained to match often looks better than any factory piece.

blocks.text: Fixing the height problem before it becomes a trip hazard

items.text: Not the subfloor, the finished floor. A 5.5 mm plank on 1.5 mm pad is 7 mm. Porcelain on backer board is often 12 to 14 mm. That difference decides the strip.
Raise the vinyl side with thicker underlayment or a plywood shim, or accept a ramp. In older Seattle houses with sagging floors we often shim under the plank near the doorway.

items.d: Put the transition under the door
items.text: With the door closed, the strip should hide beneath it so each room reads as one floor. The vinyl often runs a few inches past the room it belongs to.
Where vinyl meets tile in a bathroom or the slab at a basement door, run color-matched silicone in the gap under the strip. It keeps mop water and tracked rain out of the seam.

blocks.text: Can you skip transitions in an open plan?

a.title: Reasonable when
items: Vinyl runs continuously room to room with no other floor in between
Total run is under the manufacturer's limit, often 40 to 50 ft each way
The core is rigid SPC and the subfloor is flat through the doorways

b.title: Required when
items: Any change of material, even to a different vinyl
Runs beyond the manufacturer limit, or an L-shaped plan with a long leg
Condo rules that ask for a break at the unit entry for sound and access

blocks.text: The transition mistakes we see most in Seattle

items.html: Screwing the strip through the planks. The floor buckles by the first hot week in August. It is the most common cause of a vinyl floor lifting at a doorway; see why vinyl plank floors lift and peak.
Running the vinyl tight to the tile with no gap. It looks clean on install day and gaps or peaks by winter. Leave the gap and cover it.
Using a metal carpet bar at a vinyl edge. That is the fix for old sheet vinyl, not plank. The matching end cap costs little and is the difference between a remodel and a rental.
Ignoring door swing and appliance paths. A tall threshold at a Wallingford kitchen door catches the dishwasher on delivery day and the door every day.
Matching the strip to the wrong floor. Where vinyl meets original oak, a strip in the oak's color disappears. A vinyl-colored strip against real wood looks like a patch.

blocks.text: What to settle before the installer arrives

items: Walk every doorway and note what the vinyl will meet: tile, carpet, wood, slab or more vinyl.
Have the installer measure finished heights at each opening and name the strip that goes where.
Order transitions in the plank's dye lot, or plan a stained hardwood threshold where vinyl meets real wood.
Decide where the seam lands. Under the door is the goal, and it changes how much plank each room needs.
In a Seattle condo, check the HOA flooring rules; some require a transition at the entry and a specific underlayment.
Ask whether doors will be undercut and baseboards removed, since both affect how clean the edges look.

faq.q: Do you need a transition strip between vinyl plank and tile?
faq.a: Almost always. Even when the two floors land at the same height, the vinyl needs an expansion gap at the tile edge, and a T-molding covers it. If the tile is higher, use a reducer or threshold. The exception is glue-down vinyl, which does not float and can be caulked to the tile.

faq.q: How do you transition vinyl plank to carpet?
faq.a: With an end cap, also called a square nose. The cap fastens to the subfloor at the vinyl edge, and the carpet is stretched, trimmed and tucked against it over its own tack strip. Never lay the carpet over the vinyl, and never pin the vinyl under the tack strip.

faq.q: What is the difference between a T-molding and a reducer?
faq.a: A T-molding bridges two floors of equal height, with its stem in the gap between them. A reducer ramps from a higher floor down to a lower one. Under about 1/8 in of difference, use a T-molding; beyond that, a reducer or threshold so nobody trips.

faq.q: Can vinyl plank run through a doorway without a transition?
faq.a: Yes, if it is the same vinyl on both sides, the total run stays under the manufacturer's limit, and the subfloor is flat through the opening. Rigid SPC cores handle long open runs better than WPC or flexible plank. Any change of material needs a strip.

faq.q: How much gap should vinyl plank have at a transition?
faq.a: Follow the manufacturer, usually 1/4 to 3/8 in on each side of the strip track. The strip covers the gap. In Seattle homes with south-facing glass or radiant heat, use the larger figure, because heat drives most of the movement in vinyl plank.
